scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4521: Hi IT, our internet in the CS department keeps
BLINKING. Every now and then, totally at random, everything freezes for a few
seconds and then comes back like nothing happened -- our gateway is the
192.168.2.1 thing. Something around the router port our department hangs off
must be going wrong, but I don't know which bit. Could someone look at the
port that does 192.168.2.1 and make it stop blinking? Thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0's CS-segment interface holds
  192.168.2.1 and responds steadily; CS hosts reach the gateway with 0% loss and
  there are no interface flaps. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of a gateway "flap" that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the 192.168.2.1 gateway
intermittently dropping due to a flapping/overloaded router0 interface -- is NOT
reproducible: cs_hod reaches 192.168.2.1 with 0% loss, router0's CS-segment
interface is up and stable, ripd is running, and there is no flap script, no
carrier-transition history, and no relevant log churn.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the gateway is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("drops at random")
is done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean ping does not clear it, but
the absence of any flap process, carrier transitions, or interface errors does. A
correct agent checks the gateway and interface state/counters and finds it steady.
An agent that "finds" a flap -- blaming router0, an interface, or a load issue to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: Layer-3 routing between the CS LAN (192.168.2.0/24) and the “internet” segment (128.168.0.0/16) is missing. The CS gateway port itself (router0 eth1) and the access switch (switch1) are healthy; the fault lies in the routing control plane on the transit router.

Mechanism: CS hosts send traffic to gateway 192.168.2.1 (router0). Router0 has no route beyond its directly connected networks, so it returns ICMP “Destination Net Unreachable.” To users this appears as brief freezes while applications retry, then “comes back” when traffic is to reachable subnets or after timeouts.

Localization: 
- Router0 (gateway 192.168.2.1): FRR/RIP is running, but its routing table contains only connected routes; no route to 128.168.0.0/16 or any upstream default (verified by “show ip route” and “ip route”). 
- From cs_lab2 to pc5 (128.168.0.5) we receive “From 192.168.2.1 Destination Net Unreachable,” proving the drop at router0 due to missing route. 
- Router1 (the transit between 10.10.0.0/8 and 20.20.0.0/8) has FRR running but no routing configuration; its table shows only connected networks, so it cannot learn or propagate routes from router2. 
- Physical layer: router0 eth1 and switch1 ports are UP, no flaps/errors; STP on switch1 is forwarding on both ports.

Root cause: Router1 lacks any dynamic routing (RIP) or static routes, so router0 never learns a path to the internet networks behind router2.

Corrective fix: Enable RIP on router1 for 10.0.0.0/8 and 20.0.0.0/8 (and optionally its 192.168.3.0/24 and 192.168.4.0/24), or add a static default route on router0 to 10.10.0.2 and corresponding routes on router1 toward 20.20.0.2. After this, router0 will learn 128.168.0.0/16 (and/or a default) via router1→router2, restoring consistent internet reachability from the CS LAN.
